articles.title: Kavanaugh throws Trump 'a lifeline' on mail ballot rules despite Supreme Court loss before midterms
articles.summary: The Supreme Court denied Trump's emergency request, but Justice Brett Kavanaugh's concurrence signals the USPS rule may survive for 2028.
articles.body: Brett Kavanaugh, President Donald Trump's "hero" Supreme Court justice, isn't closing the door on the United States Postal Service (USPS) enacting Trump's ballot-mail rules in the future, although he agreed with the majority that implementing them ahead of the 2026 midterm elections is too soon. "In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority," Kavanaugh wrote in his concurring opinion in United States Postal Service, et al. v. California, et al. The concurrence comes roughly three months after Kavanaugh laid out a legal pathway for Trump to implement his executive order curtailing birthright citizenship in his concurrence in Trump v. Barbara. Kavanaugh also offered a blueprint for implementing Trump's sweeping tariffs in his dissent in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump. "I would note though that Justice Kavanaugh threw the government a lifeline by saying that he views it as likely that they do have the statutory authority. And I think if you read the dissent, you can see where Justices Thomas and Alito are on questions like that as well," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, told Fox News Digital. TRUMP BLASTS SUPREME COURT 'DISASTER' AFTER JUSTICES RULE AGAINST HIM ON MAIL-IN VOTING The Supreme Court on Monday denied the Trump administration’s emergency request to lift a lower court injunction blocking the U.S. Postal Service rule, ruling that the government was "unlikely to succeed on the merits" of its challenge. The decision leaves the rule blocked for the 2026 midterms after ballots have already been sent. But as the litigation continues, the case could return to the Supreme Court. "I think there's a fair chance that it winds back up in front of the Supreme Court eventually," Snead told Fox News Digital. A dissent written by Justice Samuel Alito and joined by Justice Clarence Thomas also raised questions about whether the policy could ultimately survive the legal challenge and take effect before 2028. "I do think that as a practical matter, the rule is not going to be implemented in time for the midterms. I think that's a done deal at this point. But I do hold out hope that there will be some additional litigation over this that could allow this rule to be implementing ahead of the 2028 presidential election," Snead said. The Postal Service rule requires federal ballot-mail envelopes to include an election-mail logo, be scannable by high-speed processing equipment, and carry a specialized barcode unique to each voter. States would also have to upload certain voter information to a Postal Service portal. A coalition of 24 Democratic state attorneys general sued the Trump administration, alleging the rule violates the Constitution's Elections Clause, which grants Congress the power to regulate elections. The Trump administration argued the USPS is regulating the mail, not election procedures. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS "So this case is still alive and well, and I think that Kavanaugh has given us all some hope that as it progresses eventually, this rule might be allowed to go into effect hopefully in time for the 2028 election since the left has successfully killed it for 2026," Snead continued. Iowa Solicitor General Eric Wessan also pointed to timing as a major factor, noting that earlier litigation and an injunction in Massachusetts delayed the Postal Service’s ability to publish the final rule. "So I'm not surprised now, close to the deadline when ballots have to go out to people that the Supreme Court took the approach of maintaining the status quo, although I think that Justice Alito's dissent highlights a lot of issues with the approach taken by the majority, and I would not be sure that the same result would be what the Supreme Court reaches in advance of, for example, the 2028 election," Wessan said. Alito, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented, arguing that the government had made the necessary showing for a stay. He also questioned whether some plaintiffs had standing and described that those plaintiffs relying on a "Hail Mary pass" the Supreme Court has previously said "rarely succeeds." FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS "The hail mary passes seem to be succeeding to a certain extent," Wessan said. "So the president's executive order was issued five months ago, and the injunction followed pretty shortly after. And as the Supreme Court recognized in the litigation earlier, that injunction against the executive order was improper." "But the amount of time that it took to get that resolved by the Supreme Court put the Postal Service in a very tough spot timing-wise with rolling it out for the election coming up in November, especially because states are on the verge of having to send ballots out, whether to the armed services or otherwise," Wessan continued. Abhishek Kambil said the lack of a fuller explanation from the court’s majority stood out to him. "I think the biggest surprise was the fact that it came with an unreasoned order, especially right after they granted a stay in Missouri, which was also on an unreasoned order. So, in cases like this, where there's a lot at stake, you would hope that in a stay opinion that the Supreme Court would explain its reasoning," Kambil said. JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER "So, I think the biggest thing that surprised me was the lack of explanation, especially given Justice Alito had a pretty methodical dissent explaining all the ways the majority got wrong, and we don't know exactly how the majority decided to deny the stay," Kambil told Fox News Digital. Wessan said that he expects the rule to remain sidelined this year while leaving open the possibility of a different outcome later. "This rule won't be in effect for the 2026 election, but it very well may end up in effect for the 2028 election, and this is just one of many actions the administration is taking to help with voter integrity," Wessan said. Snead argued that without a looming election, Democratic states may have a tougher time fighting against implementing the USPS rules. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "So they're going to have a difficult time and a steeper hill to climb if they're trying to explain in 2027, for instance, why they can't possibly comply with basic rules like this over a two-year time frame," Snead told Fox News Digital. "And just so folks understand what we're talking about. We're talking about taking best practices about mail ballot envelope design that have been long-standing and making that mandatory guidance." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And we're also talking about getting lists of eligible mail voters that states already have so that the Postal Service can essentially create manifests and that will allow them to know who they're sending ballots to, and it will allow those ballots to be tracked. So this is a very basic, very simple thing," Snead continued.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers unhappy with lack of progress on Iran war
articles.summary: Senate Republicans aren’t happy with the lack of progress in the Iran war and what they say is the administration’s failure to identify clear objectives to end the conflict. The war continues to be a major drag on GOP candidates as the failure to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and new threats facing oil exports…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans aren’t happy with the lack of progress in the Iran war and what they say is the administration’s failure to identify clear objectives to end the conflict.

The war continues to be a major drag on GOP candidates as the failure to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and new threats facing oil exports from Iranian-backed Houthi militias have sent the prices to nearly $106 a barrel, while raising the national gas price average to $4.37 a gallon.

But Republicans are particularly concerned about the war’s impact on the price of diesel, which has soared to a national average of $6.31 and hit several Senate battleground states — including Alaska, Nebraska, Iowa and Maine — especially hard.

Some Republicans are now floating the idea of embargoing diesel exports produced in the United States to lower prices.

Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) expressed frustration over “the lack of just transparency and information from the administration on what’s happening, what we should expect, the costs,” joining other GOP senators who have expressed similar grievances.

Murkowski said senators received a cost estimate for the conflict from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth just before the August recess but haven’t had any significant updates since then.

“I don’t think that the president ever really made the case for, ‘This is why I’m going into Iran now, this is the objective, these will be the metrics along the way,’” she said. “I don’t think that was ever fully articulated.”

“As I’m talking to Alaskans, they’re saying, ‘Wait a minute, he said we were going to be in and out in a matter of weeks. And not only are we still there but this is what I am feeling in my community when it comes to the cost of the war,’” she added. “I’m not satisfied with where we are. Not at all.”

Murkowski’s colleague Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) faces a tough reelection race in what is now a key race for the GOP.

President Trump said in March the conflict would likely last only four or five weeks. Instead, it has dragged on for nearly seven months.

He declared “total and complete victory” early on but has not reached a peace deal to resume oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), a member of the Armed Services Committee, said voters “would love to hear a clear message coming from the administration” about the war’s objectives and the plan for ending it.

Ernst said voters are particularly concerned about high fuel prices.

“They don’t want to see ground troops going in but certainly they do believe in having a non-nuclear capable Iran,” she said.

Two House Republicans from battleground districts in Iowa voted Wednesday with five other Republicans and Democrats to pass a war powers resolution directing Trump to end the conflict with Iran.

GOP Reps. Zach Nunn (Iowa) and Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa) voted for the resolution after previously voting against it, underscoring the mounting pressure on Republicans in swing states and districts.

Recent polls show the Iowa Senate race between Democratic state legislator Josh Turek and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) is very close — with some polls showing Turek ahead by a few points and others showing Hinson in the lead.

Sen. Susan Collins (R), who faces a tough race in Maine, said Iran posed a national security threat, but she faulted Hegseth for failing to fully anticipate the leverage Iran would have if it shut the critical Strait of Hormuz for months.

“There’s no doubt that Iran is the greatest sponsor of terrorist groups around the world, is pursuing a nuclear weapon, and has an extensive inventory — or did — of ballistic missiles. Having said all of that, it does not appear to me that the secretary of Defense or War had a clear plan,” she said, referring to Hegseth.

“For example, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz should have been anticipated. It happened during the Iraq-Iran war and it’s an obvious point of leverage but there doesn’t seem to have been any plan for it,” Collins said.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said voters in Utah are overwhelmingly concerned with “affordability” and are linking “gas prices” to the war.

But he declined to comment on the administration’s handling of the conflict, saying that’s “an hourlong answer.”

Polls show that a large majority of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war and think it was a mistake to start the conflict.

A New York Times/Siena poll of 1,503 voters conducted from Sept. 8-13 found that 66 percent of likely voters disapprove of the war while only 31 percent approve.

The survey also found that 63 percent of voters think Trump’s decision to go to war was the wrong decision while only 32 percent think it was the right move.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said public support is weak for the conflict in part because of the president’s failure to clearly articulate his plans and objectives.

“I support the president’s efforts there, I just wish we had a better articulation about what exactly our objectives were,” he said.

“If the president was clearer on what the objectives were that we were trying to achieve, I think [constituents] would be more patient. But in the absence of that, I think there’s just confusion,” the Texas senator added. “I think if we had a little bit better articulation of what the goals are I think we’d have better acceptance.”

The war is affecting Saudi Arabia’s ability to ship oil through the Red Sea, which could raise oil and gas prices even higher. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have seized strategically important islands near Red Sea shipping lanes and damaged an important oil pipeline that Saudi Arabia had used as an alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the Trump administration is doing a good job putting economic pressure on Iran with sanctions and a naval blockade, but he warned the spread of the conflict through Houthi militias is troubling.

“The problem of course is the strait and now the Red Sea,” he said. “I don’t know what our military response is going to be with respect to the Houthis.”

“The Houthis are dug in those mountains pretty well. I would hope that the other countries in the Middle East would help, and I would hope that other countries in the world would help but I don’t know if they will or not,” he added.

articles.title: Ocasio-Cortez sees confidence in her White House chances grow
articles.summary: Confidence is growing among some influential Democrats about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) prospects in the 2028 presidential race. The New York Democrat has quickly become one of the party’s most prominent voices, tapping into a surge of populist energy on the left while growing her following as Democrats search for a leader nearly two years after…
articles.body:
Confidence is growing among some influential Democrats about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) prospects in the 2028 presidential race.

The New York Democrat has quickly become one of the party’s most prominent voices, tapping into a surge of populist energy on the left while growing her following as Democrats search for a leader nearly two years after their crushing 2024 losses.

Some Democrats are even drawing comparisons to former President Obama’s insurgent 2008 campaign — and the grassroots campaign that helped catapult him to the presidency.

“If she raises her hand … the number of volunteers will be nothing like we’ve seen since 2007,” Robert Wolf, the longtime Democratic donor who hosted Obama’s first fundraiser in New York in 2007, said during a conversation on The Hill Insider’s Fight for 2028 .

“The young people are going to come out in droves, and I think it would literally change the field overnight,” he said. “And if she doesn’t run, then it’s going to be a totally different race.”

“AOC has been really interesting to watch the last few months,” Wolf continued, using the congresswoman’s nickname. “I find myself interested in seeing what she says and does.”

Democratic strategists also say those in their party are taking notice of Ocasio-Cortez’s strengths.

“I think she has continued to show over the past few years that she has very sharp political and policy skills that every month more people are realizing what they thought about her was partially a caricature,” said Democratic strategist Eddie Vale. “And when you combine that with her generational talent for communicating in a way and on platforms that most Democrats still struggle with, her stock is definitely going to keep rising.”

In recent weeks, Ocasio-Cortez has aimed at appealing to voters beyond the Democratic base. She’s also sought to evolve her image — perhaps with an eye on skeptics.

In an appearance on ABC News’s “This Week” in August, Ocasio-Cortez quoted a New York City Council member, saying, “Woke 1 was crazy,” before laughing.

The moment was a signal, Democrats concluded, that she was trying to appeal beyond her base.

“That to me said she has her mind on higher office,” one strategist said. “Whether that’s running for Senate or running for the presidency, it was a definite nod to folks who might be skeptical about her.”

Ocasio-Cortez also garnered headlines for her public conversation on freezing her eggs. For days, as she gained thousands of followers on her social media platforms, she took viewers along her personal journey, even filming herself administering fertility injections and posting the videos to Instagram.

If she does run for president, Democrats say, she would kick off her campaign with a huge advantage.

For starters, she’s among the most recognizable politicians with strong name ID and a huge social media following. She can easily draw a crowd, easily luring earned media.

She is also one of the party’s most prolific fundraisers.

In a fundraising appeal to her supporters this week to help candidates win the House and Senate, she nodded to all the interest that she’s been getting on her political prospects.

Ocasio-Cortez said she knows “there’s a lot of speculation right now about what I’ll decide to do in 2028.”

“I get asked about it in nearly every interview and at every event. In some ways, I understand the interest,” the congresswoman said.

Democrats say Ocasio-Cortez could own the progressive lane right out of the gate, even though some others — including Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) — are openly flirting with a run and are already starting to recruit staff.

They also say the new Democratic map of primary states could play in her favor, particularly with Nevada, New Mexico and Michigan among the first five states to vote.

“What’s happening now is a lot of folks are approaching AOC with a little more openness because they’re saying this moment may call for someone who has that credibility with progressives at a time when progressives are having a moment,” said one longtime Democratic strategist.

Still, that strategist warned that the New Yorker must thread the needle carefully so she doesn’t lose the electorate that elevated her in the first place.

“She has more credibility with mainstream voices than she ever has, but there’s a risk in that because she can’t alienate her base. She needs to hold credibility with that base,” the strategist said.

The strategist and others pointed to the rise of democratic socialists as potentially problematic for Ocasio-Cortez. During her reelection campaign in 2024, for example, the national chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America withdrew their endorsement of her because some of its members felt as though her views were not aligned with their positions on Israel and Palestine.

Other strategists still question whether a progressive candidate can win nationally in a presidential election.

“I will go to my grave emphasizing that while it may work in a city like New York or in a Democratic-leaning district, it’s not going to work in swing states we need to win,” said one longtime Democratic operative.

But Vale underscored that the Democratic primary is still wide open.

“Like everyone else right now, their positives and minuses are mostly just on paper, and the real test will be how long they can stand up in the long slog of actual primaries,” he said.

articles.title: Talarico neck and neck with Paxton in new Texas Senate poll
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico, a state lawmaker, and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton remain deadlocked in the Texas Senate race less than seven weeks out from Election Day, according to a new poll released Thursday. The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey found 47 percent of state voters supported Talarico, while 46 percent backed Paxton in this race. …
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico, a state lawmaker, and Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton remain deadlocked in the Texas Senate race less than seven weeks out from Election Day, according to a new poll released Thursday.

The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey found 47 percent of state voters supported Talarico, while 46 percent backed Paxton in this race.

The Democrat has gained a slight lead over the GOP state attorney general in recent polling. In a Telemundo/Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey released earlier this week, the Democrat posted a three-point advantage over his GOP opponent.

Talarico and Paxton tied in two separate Siena University polls in June. Talarico pulled ahead of Paxton by four percentage points in this polling center’s survey at the end of July.

In the Texas gubernatorial race, incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) garnered 49 percent of support in the poll, compared to the 46 percent who supported Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa.

Additionally, the survey asked Texas voters about their opinion on the GOP’s midterm convention earlier this month in Dallas, where President Trump and other party leaders urged Republicans to turn out the vote this November.

Among the voters who had heard about the two-day event, 59 percent of Republicans and 53 percent of Democrats said the convention made them more excited to cast their ballot in this election.

Sixty-eight percent of independent voters in this poll said the convention had “no impact” on their excitement to vote.

The economy remained a top concern for voters, with 36 percent of Texans ranking this as a top issue ahead of immigration, education, healthcare and threats to democracy.

The Hill/Emerson poll was conducted among a sample of 1,000 likely voters in the state from Sept. 12-14 with a margin of error of approximately 3 percentage points.

articles.title: El-Sayed narrowly leads Rogers in Michigan Senate race: Poll
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed holds a slight lead over his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a new poll shows. The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey released Thursday found that El-Sayed garnered 48 percent support and Rogers received 46 percent, while 4 percent of respondents remained undecided and 2…
articles.body:
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed holds a slight lead over his opponent , former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a new poll shows.

The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey released Thursday found that El-Sayed garnered 48 percent support and Rogers received 46 percent, while 4 percent of respondents remained undecided and 2 percent chose another candidate in the race to succeed outgoing Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

Of the 1,000 Michiganders polled, Spencer Kimball, the executive director of Emerson College Polling, noted “there’s a substantial educational divide in the Senate race.”

“Voters without a four-year degree favor Rogers, 48 percent to 45 percent, while college graduates support El-Sayed, 53 percent to 42 percent,” he added.

El-Sayed led among respondents who identified as independents at around 47.5 percent support to Rogers’s 44.8 percent. Rogers, meanwhile, led El-Sayed among respondents 40 years old and above.

Rogers and El-Sayed are battling in one of seven Senate races that the election handicapper Cook Political Report rates as a “toss-up.”

In the Wolverine State’s gubernatorial election, the Democratic nominee, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, held a 7 point lead over her opponent, Rep. John James (R-Mich.), at 49 percent support and 42 percent, respectively. Three percent of respondents favored someone else, and 6 percent were undecided. Candidates are running to replace term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D), who is seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender.

Respondents were also asked if they held a favorable or unfavorable view of all candidates in the Senate race.

Forty-nine percent of respondents held a favorable view of El-Sayed, compared to 42 percent who favored Rogers. Forty-four percent of pollsters had an unfavorable view of El-Sayed, while 46 percent viewed Rogers unfavorably. The remaining 7 percent indicated they were neutral or never heard of El-Sayed and 12 percent responded the same for Rogers.

The candidates were slated to participate in a debate with Detroit’s Fox affiliate Tuesday, but Rogers’ campaign pulled out due to “media bias” — citing the debate’s moderator journalist Roop Raj.

“Roop Raj has made his position clear, from praising Abdul as ‘brilliant,’ to being celebrated by Hasan Piker as ‘my GOAT,’ and bragging about his political stunts,” Alyssa Brouillet, the Rogers campaign’s communications director said in a statement .

Despite Rogers’s absence from Tuesday’s debate, El-Sayed attended, standing beside an empty podium.

Thursday’s poll was conducted between Sept. 12-14 among 1,000 likely Michigan voters and had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

articles.title: Dem megadonor unleashes reality check on Harris for 2028 while eying socialist firebrand
articles.summary: Reid Hoffman, a top Silicon Valley donor, calls another Kamala Harris 2028 presidential run a "very challenging path" while expressing surprising openness to supporting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
articles.body: One of Kamala Harris' biggest billionaire backers in 2024 is already casting doubt on another White House bid — while showing surprising openness to a potential 2028 contender from a very different corner of the Democratic Party. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman called another Harris presidential run a "very challenging path" Wednesday before leaving the door open to supporting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and describing the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic." "It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked during POLITICO's Decoded Summit Wednesday in the nation's capital whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for." The comments mark a notable contrast for Hoffman, who poured millions of dollars into helping elect Harris in 2024 and rallied other Silicon Valley donors behind her campaign after former President Joe Biden ended his re-election bid. Asked Wednesday whether Harris should try again in 2028, Hoffman pointed to what he expects to be a crowded Democratic field. WATCH: AOC WON'T RULE OUT WHITE HOUSE BID AFTER POLL NAMES HER DEMOCRATS' TOP 2028 PICK "I think it would be a very challenging path for her, and it's going to be a very noisy field," Hoffman said in response. KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY Hoffman's answer was not an endorsement, however. He said any potential support for Ocasio-Cortez would depend in part on whom she was running against, before Hoffman laid out the qualities he would look for in a candidate. "If you're basically kind of pro-society, which she is, and pro-business, which is a question, that tends to be where I think the right focal points are," Hoffman said. Meanwhile, two years earlier, Hoffman had made a similar case for Harris, pitching her to hundreds of venture capitalists as "a great centrist" who cared about both society and business, according to a report from The Washington Post. "She is a great centrist in that she cares about a greater society and cares about business," Hoffman said during a virtual "VCs for Harris" rally in 2024, according to The Washington Post. Hoffman’s comments this week about Harris' potential 2028 bid also came days after California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he would not seek the presidency if Harris entered the 2028 race. Republican strategist Mark Bednar, who previously worked for then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, interpreted the two developments as early signs of uncertainty surrounding Harris' position in the emerging Democratic field. GAVIN NEWSOM SAYS HE WON'T RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 IF KAMALA HARRIS RUNS "The idea of pouring cold water over Kamala for others to step forward seems to be very real," Bednar told Fox News Digital. "I don't know if it's directly connected to Newsom in that instance, but it's super interesting how it happens the day after." Bednar, meanwhile, described Newsom's comments about his potential 2028 presidential run as a "smoke signal to Democratic donors" that "you guys are going to have to be the ones that be the bad cop here because I'm just going to be the good cop in public." articles.title: The Fed just threw a wrench in Trump's midterm economic message
articles.summary: Kevin Warsh's first rate hike as Fed chair defies President Donald Trump's repeated push for lower borrowing costs ahead of midterm elections.
articles.body: With the midterms looming, President Donald Trump wants lower interest rates to ease the squeeze on American families. Instead, the Federal Reserve raised rates on Wednesday. The decision is aimed at combating stubborn inflation, but it will make borrowing more expensive for voters and delivers a big hit to Trump's economic promises with less than two months until Americans cast their ballots and determine which party will control Congress. The Fed does not set the prices of groceries, cars or homes. But its decisions affect how much Americans pay to borrow money, especially when they buy a house or car. Higher rates can add hundreds of dollars to monthly payments, even when the price of the home or vehicle has not changed. ONE LITTLE-KNOWN MEETING HELPS DECIDE WHAT AMERICANS CAN AFFORD — AND WHAT THEY CAN’T The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point Wednesday, bringing it to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The increase — the Fed’s first in three years — was aimed at slowing inflation, which remains above the central bank’s 2% goal. Higher energy prices and tariffs have added to pressure on household budgets, and the Fed’s projections indicate that another rate increase could come later this year if inflation remains elevated. The rate hike puts Kevin Warsh, Trump’s pick to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, at odds with the president’s push for lower borrowing costs. The decision could strain their relationship and revive memories of Trump’s repeated clashes with former Fed Chair Jerome Powell. TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE Although the president appoints members of the Fed’s Board of Governors, the FOMC is designed to make rate decisions based on economic conditions rather than political pressure. Warsh underscored that independence Wednesday, saying the Fed acted based on its assessment of employment, the strength of the economy and the inflation outlook. WARSH FACES FIRST BIG TEST ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRUMP’S FED VISION COMES INTO FOCUS The Fed chairman was later asked what message he had for Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower rates. He declined to discuss the president, saying, "I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president." The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For Trump, the timing is difficult. He campaigned on improving affordability, but the rate increase could make it harder for households to feel financial relief — and for the administration to show voters that its economic promises are producing results. With affordability and the cost of living already central issues in the midterm elections, higher borrowing costs could further complicate the president’s economic message.

articles.title: Trump wants largest-ever Israeli heavy bomb transfer — but proposal has Congress preparing for $2.8B fight
articles.summary: The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs for Israel, drawing fierce opposition from Bernie Sanders and Chris Van Hollen in Congress.
articles.body: The Trump administration is preparing a $2.8 billion military aid package for Israel that would include 40,000 heavy bombs, according to multiple reports. It would be the largest proposed transfer of the powerful munitions to Israel in recent years, if it clears Congress. The proposed package includes 20,000 unguided bombs designed to destroy buildings and bunkers, known as MK-84 bombs, and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs, which are warhead versions fitted with precision-guidance kits — both bombs are 2,000 pounds per unit. Additionally, according to Reuters and The Washington Post, the proposal includes 20,000 much-tougher I-2000 penetrator warheads, which are designed to penetrate concrete or underground facilities before exploding. The package, which is not yet final, has been informally communicated to congressional committees that review major U.S. arms sales — and it's already drawing opposition from Democratic lawmakers. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is calling on Congress to reject the White House's proposal, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., vowed that lawmakers will "work to stop it." HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL "The American people are sick and tired of funding Israel's genocide in Gaza," Sanders wrote on social media, accusing the Trump administration of "doubling down" by providing $2.8 billion in bombs to the Israeli government. "Not acceptable. Congress must reject these agreements." Van Hollen similarly criticized the proposed package and its use of U.S. taxpayer funds, writing, "How is this America First? We will work to stop it." The State Department did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Israel's Ministry of Defense declined to weigh in. "All foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process. We do not comment on pending sales," a senior administration official told Fox News Digital. Most of the package would be financed through Foreign Military Financing, which uses congressionally appropriated U.S. funds for eligible allies to purchase American-made defense equipment. If completed, the package would be the largest single sale of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in recent years. It would exceed a 2025 sale that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The Trump administration approved that nearly $3 billion sale after bypassing the normal congressional review process. It's unclear whether that bypass could or will be used again this time around. The weapons were at the center of a previous U.S. policy dispute, as well. During President Joe Biden's term, his administration paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel in 2024 over concerns of the potential for mass casualties in densely populated Gaza. President Donald Trump lifted that hold after returning to office. TRUMP CONFIRMS ‘CRAZY’ NETANYAHU CLASH AS QUESTIONS MOUNT OVER PUSH TO HOLD FIRE ON HEZBOLLAH TERRORISTS The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants designed for different targets, including hardened and underground structures. Israel has used U.S.-made heavy munitions during its military operations in Gaza and Lebanon, while the United States has used similar weapons against hardened targets in previous conflicts. The proposed transfer comes as Israel remains engaged on multiple fronts. Israeli forces have continued strikes against Hamas in Gaza despite a fragile ceasefire, while tensions with Hezbollah persist following fighting in Lebanon. The United States and Israel also conducted military operations against Iran earlier this year. The package remains at an early stage of the U.S. arms sales process. Informal congressional notification allows relevant committees to review a proposed transfer before the administration proceeds to formal notification. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If the administration formally notifies Congress, lawmakers would have an opportunity to review the proposal under the Arms Export Control Act and could pursue legislation seeking to block the sale.

articles.title: Harris joins forces with radical Senate nominee in key swing state as 2028 whispers swirl
articles.summary: Kamala Harris joins Abdul El-Sayed at a Michigan fundraiser on Black maternal health, raising questions about a potential 2028 presidential run.
articles.body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is set to join Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at an upcoming roundtable in Michigan, according to his campaign. The two will appear at a Black maternal health roundtable next Tuesday, raising questions about whether Harris might be trying to court the progressive wing of the party in preparation for a 2028 presidential run. "I’m just really looking forward to having her here, and she is somebody who so many folks in communities like Detroit look up to as an inspirational leader," El-Sayed told Politico in an interview on Wednesday. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN "I’m grateful that she’s coming in and having conversations about what it takes to get the turnout up, so that we can get on to working on some of these issues in the U.S. Senate," he continued. The scheduled roundtable comes after Harris endorsed El-Sayed last month, praising his stance on issues like affordability. "Dr. Abdul El-Sayed understands the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election. While Michiganders struggle to afford everyday essentials — housing, gas, groceries, health care and child care — Trump and Republicans in Congress are giving away $1 trillion in tax breaks to the wealthy and powerful," Harris wrote. "Abdul knows that we need bold solutions to the crises facing America’s working families and he is ready to take on this fight," Harris continued. "I proudly stand with him to ensure we win a Democratic Senate majority in Nov." The news of Harris' upcoming visit to Michigan comes as The Detroit News, a prominent Michigan newspaper, endorsed El-Sayed's Republican rival, Mike Rogers, for Senate on Wednesday. "Mike Rogers is the prototype of a United States Senator," the paper said in its endorsement, referencing his 14 years in the House, Army career, and private sector experience dealing with cybersecurity. On the other hand, the paper skewered El-Sayed for his radical rhetoric, saying he "has worked so hard covering his tracks leading up to this Senate race that it's impossible to know who he really is or where he would stand in the Senate." "He has deleted social media posts that reportedly called into question his attitude about America in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. He's taken down roughly 100 YouTube videos that paint an unflattering picture of him and his cultural views," the paper concluded. "A candidate who feels the need to hide his past from voters is not someone who can be trusted to be the same person after Election Day as he was on the campaign trail." In addition to Harris' visit, El-Sayed is expected to have a busy final stretch of his campaign before the November election as he attends multiple fundraisers in California and New York. In late September, El-Sayed is scheduled to attend a Hollywood fundraiser at the home of George Soros' nephew, Jeffrey Soros, who is a movie producer. In addition to Soros and his wife, the host committee includes several Obama alums, including Crooked Media's "Pod Save America" hosts Tommy Vietor and Jon Favreau. Ben Rhodes, the failed architect of Obama's Iran deal, is also on the host committee. El-Sayed will also be visiting San Francisco during this West Coast swing. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK Next month, El-Sayed will also be going to New York City to attend a fundraiser hosted by several far-left activists, where the price to attend ranges from $250 to $57,800. Harris’ endorsement of El-Sayed marks just her second major progressive candidate endorsement in the 2026 midterms. She is also supporting Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in Maine who is backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Before the midterms, Harris also supported New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who was also DSA-endorsed, but only stated that she "supported the Democrat in the race." For his own part, El-Sayed has rejected terms like "progressive" and "moderate" and is not backed by the DSA. But like Mamdani, El-Sayed has made affordability — and the role of government — key pieces of his campaign. In addition to calling for lowering housing costs, he’s advocated for Medicare for All, opposes corporate tax carve-outs, and he supports tuition-free access to higher education. Harris has also received support from El-Sayed in the past. Notably, after now-former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 election, El-Sayed called on the party to rally behind Harris, citing her "potential" for leadership. "Considering all the dangers of the Republican nominee … it’s time for all of us to unite behind Kamala Harris to defeat Trump," El-Sayed wrote in a post in July 2024. articles.title: Homeowners in the heart of America’s AI boom are getting an unexpected payoff
articles.summary: Loudoun County homeowners save $5,800 a year in property taxes thanks to data centers, which generate 45% of all local tax revenue on just 3% of land.
articles.body: Billions in build-outs of facilities to support the artificial intelligence (AI) boom have become a lightning rod in communities across America, but homeowners in the nation’s data center capital are seeing a surprising payoff — thousands of dollars in property tax relief. The massive projects have emerged as an issue in the 2026 midterm elections, as voters raise concerns about electricity costs, water use, land development and the strain on local infrastructure. Opposition has crossed party lines, forcing candidates to confront an industry that state and local governments spent years courting. Yet just outside Washington, D.C., the richest U.S. enclave of Loudoun County, Virginia, offers a striking case study of the industry's economic upside. Home to the sprawling tech corridor known as "Data Center Alley," Loudoun has the highest concentration of data centers in the world. Decades of development have transformed the county's landscape and dramatically expanded its tax base, offering a real-world look at the financial benefits proponents say the industry can bring to local communities. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS "Loudoun County has more data centers than anywhere else in the country. It's been sort of the capital of data center development for decades," Jared Walczak, vice president of state projects at the Tax Foundation, told Fox News Digital. "And because of that, Loudoun County property taxes are about half of what they would be without data centers. In fact, data centers provide about 45% of all local tax revenue to Loudoun County, not just property taxes, but all local tax revenue." Walczak said the impact translates into significant savings for individual homeowners. "The average homeowner would pay $5,800 more a year in property taxes if you didn't have data center development," he said, noting that data centers occupy only about 3% of the county's land. But the rapid expansion of data centers has also fueled concerns that their enormous electricity demands could leave residents footing a higher utility bill, potentially offsetting some of those savings. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS Walczak pushed back on that worry, arguing the industry's impact on homeowners' property taxes is clearer. "The property tax relief is real, measurable and significant," he said. "The energy costs are largely a solved problem." Walczak told Fox News Digital that the increased demand could require utilities to build new generation and transmission infrastructure, while adding more customers and electricity usage can also spread the grid's fixed costs across a larger base. The critical question, he said, is who pays for the additional infrastructure. "You pay for the additional generation and transmission capacity. The data center pays for that," Walczak said. "And then you actually see a slight reduction in energy costs for everyone." He pointed again to Northern Virginia, arguing that its experience challenges fears that a heavy concentration of data centers inevitably translates into higher electricity prices for residents. "If you look at the places with the largest data center development, you actually see declines in energy prices relative to the rest of the country," Walczak said. "You look at Northern Virginia, it has lower energy prices." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As communities across the country weigh the costs and benefits of the data center boom, Walczak said Loudoun County's experience offers a glimpse at what can happen when billions of dollars in new infrastructure become part of the local tax base.

articles.title: Dos militares españoles hospitalizados tras resultar heridos por inmigrantes en Ceuta
articles.standfirst: La ministra Margarita Robles les ha visitado esta mañana en el centro sanitario de Madrid
articles.summary: La ministra Margarita Robles les ha visitado esta mañana en el centro sanitario de Madrid
articles.body: Continúa la tensión en Ceuta tras la entrada masiva de inmigrantes a la ciudad autónoma. Las últimas novedades hablan de nuevos militares allí desplegados que han sido víctimas de agresiones. Así lo ha confirmado esta mañana el propio Gobierno. Dos militares han tenido que ser evacuados de urgencia al Hospital General de la Defensa Gómez Ulla en Madrid tras sufrir agresiones por parte de inmigrantes en el marco de las labores operativas que las Fuerzas Armadas mantienen en la ciudad autónoma. La ministra de defensa Margarita Robles los ha visitado esta mañana interesándose por su estado. El propio ministerio del que ella es responsable ha evitado por el momento precisar el alcance de las lesiones, el tipo de agresiones que sufrieron y en qué momento se produjo. Lo que sí ha trascendido, según informa Antena 3, es que uno de ellos ha tenido que ser intervenido quirúrgicamente. "Nuestros militares siempre profesionales, cercanos e implicados con #Ceuta. Todo nuestro apoyo a los heridos en estas semanas, algunos incluso ingresados en el hospital Gómez Ulla, tras ser víctimas de agresiones mientras realizan su trabajo", reza el tweet que el Ministerio de Defensa publicaba en su perfil oficial de la red social X. Si bien, según informa Radio Televisión Española, fuentes conocedoras de lo sucedido han relatado que estas lesiones se produjeron “durante un altercado mientras se encontraban en cumplimiento de su misión”. Ambos estaban siendo tratados en Ceuta por diversas fracturas en las piernas y se les ha ofrecido la posibilidad de ser trasladados a Madrid, explican. Esta noticia llega justo cuando el Gobierno ha confirmado que abrirá una investigación sobre las denuncias de presuntas palizas a migrantes en Ceuta por parte de militares españoles. Decisión que se da después de que Sumar pidiese a Defensa saber más sobre estos hechos. “Nos preocupan e indignan enormemente las denuncias que estamos conociendo sobre palizas y vejaciones a personas migrantes por parte de militares que patrullan en Ceuta", dijo la portavoz Verónica Martínez Barbero.

articles.title: Republicans just got a powerful new playbook for the battle for Congress. Here's what's inside.
articles.summary: First on Fox: Advancing American Freedom unveils over 100 proposals to cut housing, energy and health care costs ahead of 2026 midterm elections.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: With control of Congress on the line and pocketbook issues dominating the campaign trail, a prominent conservative group is unveiling a sweeping affordability agenda aimed at giving Republicans a sharper economic message ahead of the November midterm elections. The Advancing American Freedom report, "Affordability 101," obtained first by Fox News Digital ahead of its Capitol Hill rollout Thursday, lays out more than 100 recommendations to lower the costs of housing, energy, food and healthcare by expanding supply, increasing competition and reducing government barriers. The blueprint is intended as a resource for Republican lawmakers and congressional staff as affordability emerges as one of the defining issues of the 2026 midterm elections. Founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, Advancing American Freedom argues costs can be lowered by reducing regulations, encouraging competition and boosting domestic production rather than creating new federal subsidies. "We want free market conservative candidates to go out there and not just put on the red jersey or not just fight against the blue jersey, but to go there and give people ideas that actually work," Advancing American Freedom President Tim Chapman told Fox News Digital. TRUMP’S AFFORDABILITY PLAN FACES CONSERVATIVE PUSHBACK AS POCKETBOOK ISSUES LOOM OVER MIDTERMS Chapman argued the size and scope of government plays a larger role in affordability than many Americans realize. "The size and scope of the government matters more than people understand in terms of its impact on the economy," Chapman said. "If you look at interest rates right now and how much of the skyrocketing interest rates is fueled by the debt and deficit problem, that's something we need to be concerned about as Americans." Many of the proposals align with Trump administration priorities, including expanding domestic energy production, building more homes, reducing regulations and encouraging innovation. But the blueprint also breaks with the administration on several issues. TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED One flashpoint is Vice President JD Vance's proposal to expand childcare subsidies by broadening eligibility under the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF), potentially providing some married families with a stay-at-home parent up to about $9,000 per child annually. "His proposal sounds great, right?" Richard Stern, vice president of the Plymouth Institute for Free Enterprise at Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "But the truth is, in many cases, it's a $9,000 divorce bonus." On housing, the report says government regulations add 26.4% to the cost of a new single-family home and calls for permitting, zoning and land-use reforms to lower construction costs. "I think those memos that deal with construction regulations and land use are the core group that would help affordability the most," Stern said. 5 STATES COULD BE THE BIGGEST LOSERS IN TRUMP'S TRADE WAR WITH CANADA, EXPERT WARNS The report also argues tariffs raise consumer prices, another point of disagreement with the administration. "If you look at your grocery bill, how much of that is impacted by tariffs?" Chapman said. "That's driving up the price of goods and it's hurting people in their pocketbooks." The blueprint also argues that expanding domestic energy production and easing regulations on artificial intelligence and data centers can help lower costs. Trump has championed rapid data center development despite growing concerns over electricity demand and local impacts. "The counties that have data centers are making money off of it," Stern said. "They're actually reducing energy prices for those homes." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As candidates sharpen their economic messages ahead of November, Chapman said the report is meant to give lawmakers concrete policy proposals they can take back to voters. "We want people to have those solutions," Chapman said. "When they go home and talk to their constituents about the future of the country, they can say, 'I actually have an idea. Here's an idea for getting interest rates down or here's an idea for more small business growth.'"

articles.title: People think they need $1.2M to retire. Here’s where that’s actually true
articles.summary: Americans think they need about $1.2 million in savings to retire comfortably, according to a survey by Schroeders published earlier this year. How far you can get with that seven-figure sum depends largely on where you live.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Americans think they need about $1.2 million in savings to retire comfortably, according to a survey by Schroders published earlier this year . How far you can get with that seven-figure sum depends largely on where you live.

In Oklahoma, $1.2 million in the bank could last you until you’re 111 if you stop working at 67. In Hawaii, you might not make it to 80 before running out of cash.

Personal finance site MoneyLion crunched the numbers on how long a hypothetical $1.2 million in retirement savings would last in every state. For each place they calculated two scenarios: if you’re collecting Social Security monthly and if you’re not collecting Social Security.

While there are several Southern and Midwestern states where a $1.2 million budget would go far for a retiree, the situation is pricier for states along the coasts.

The 10 states where $1.2 million goes furthest for retirees are:

If you’d like to stretch your retirement funds out, there are some places you definitely shouldn’t move. Even if the sandy beaches of Hawaii are calling your name, MoneyLion’s analysis found $1.2 million in retirement savings would only last around 13 years there – and that’s with Social Security to supplement.

After Hawaii, Massachusetts, California, D.C., Alaska and New York were found to be the worst places to retire on a fixed budget.

By the way, even those who think they can make it with $1.2 million in retirement savings are largely falling behind that goal. Schroders’ survey found only 30% of Americans actually believe they’ll be able to save seven figures before retirement age.

Lawmakers are debating different ways to fix Social Security’s solvency issues before the program reaches its “grow broke” date in 2032 .

Two senators who are approaching retirement themselves, Democrat Dick Durbin and Republican Bill Cassidy , have embarked on a mission to save tens of millions of Social Security beneficiaries from a projected 22% cut in their benefits that would start in just six years.

Their proposal calls for the bipartisan Social Security Advisory Board to collect public input and submit draft legislation to Congress that would keep the program’s retirement trust fund solvent for at least 50 years.

Separately, Cassidy has a proposal with Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., that calls for the creation of a $1.5 trillion fund that would be invested in stocks and other higher-risk assets over 75 years.

The seed money would be financed by the Treasury Department through additional borrowing. At the end of the 75 years, the fund’s assets would be used to repay the Treasury for the seed money as well as the borrowing that would occur over those years to keep Social Security payments going out — now projected at about $26.6 trillion.

Another idea comes from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who are calling for lifting the cap on the Social Security payroll tax.

Currently, the payroll tax that funds Social Security applies to a maximum of $184,500 in income. That means most people pay Social Security taxes on all of their income, but the wealthier do not.

“Why should a middle-class nurse pay a larger share of her paycheck than a wealthy corporate lawyer?” the two senators wrote in The New York Times.

Some conservative groups have forcefully pushed back on the idea, saying the tax increase would lead to lower wages and fewer jobs at businesses seeking to offset the additional tax burden.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Shapiro slams RFK Jr. as not ‘connected or grounded in reality’ on measles outbreak
articles.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) accused Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Wednesday of not taking adequate steps to address a growing measles outbreak in the U.S. The governor blamed the secretary, a vaccine skeptic, for the downtick in measles immunizations in the country during an appearance on CNN’s “The…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) accused Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Wednesday of not taking adequate steps to address a growing measles outbreak in the U.S.

The governor blamed the secretary, a vaccine skeptic, for the downtick in measles immunizations in the country during an appearance on CNN’s “The Source with Kaitlan Collins.”

“He doesn’t believe that measles is an issue,” Shapiro said. “When I spoke to him over the phone, he wanted to lecture me about natural measles, and in many ways, making excuses.

“He blamed Joe Biden for all of this,” Shapiro continued. “I mean, he is someone who is not, I think, connected or grounded in reality.”

The Hill has reached out to the HHS for comment.

This week, Pennsylvania’s health department reported its fourth measles-related death this year. Since January, there have been 731 total cases, including 117 new cases in the last week, according to state data .

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) does not currently report any deaths from measles. In a note on its website dashboard tracking the disease outbreak, the CDC says the National Center for Health Statistics “does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.”

The CDC has reported 3,294 confirmed measles cases across 47 states, including Pennsylvania.

After Pennsylvania health authorities reported two measles-associated deaths among unvaccinated people in August, Kennedy suggested the fatalities were fabricated to score political points.

“The performance was a replay of the Democrats’ COVID playbook: fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain,” Kennedy wrote in a social media post .

On Wednesday evening, Shapiro slammed the Trump administration for not acknowledging the deaths in Pennsylvania.

“They won’t even acknowledge these deaths on their dashboard, something that should have been an administrative process, because it doesn’t fit their phony narrative,” the governor said. “I think RFK is doing great destruction in this country by stoking this vaccine skepticism.”

Shapiro said he would not accept additional federal assistance until the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recognizes the deaths in Pennsylvania.

“I will not allow any other federal officials to come here in Pennsylvania until RFK stops meddling in the process and acknowledges the four deaths here in Pennsylvania, something he has directed his subordinates here at HHS not to acknowledge on their dashboard,” the governor said.

articles.title: Sullivan trails Peltola in Alaska Senate contest: AARP poll
articles.summary: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) trails former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) by 5 percentage points in the Alaska Senate race, according to a new poll. An AARP poll conducted by pollsters Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research released Thursday showed Peltola ahead of the GOP senator at 46 percent support to his 41 percent, with 7 percent of…
articles.body:
Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) trails former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) by 5 percentage points in the Alaska Senate race, according to a new poll.

An AARP poll conducted by pollsters Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research released Thursday showed Peltola ahead of the GOP senator at 46 percent support to his 41 percent, with 7 percent of respondents undecided.

A separate 4 percent of respondents supported Dan J. Sullivan Jr., who’s listed on the ballot as having no party affiliation, and 3 percent supported Republican Gerald Heikes.

When voters were asked whom they would choose as their second and third picks, Peltola maintains an edge in both rounds. Asked about a second pick, 50 percent of respondents said they would support the former House member while 43 percent rated the senator as their next pick.

Asked about a third choice, Peltola received 51 percent support while Sen. Sullivan received 45 percent.

Peltola performs 26 points better than Sullivan and the two other challengers among voters between the ages of 18 and 49, and she leads the senator by 32 points among independents and 18 points among women. Peltola also boasts higher enthusiasm among Democrats — 91 percent — compared with Sullivan’s performance among Republicans, which sits at 83 percent.

Meanwhile, Sullivan performs better with voters aged 50 years and older by 7 points, voters aged 65 and older by 8 points and men by 6 points.

Sullivan is fighting for a third term in the upper chamber against Peltola, who made headlines in 2022 when she defeated former Gov. Sarah Palin (R) to become the first Democrat in more than 50 years to win Alaska’s House seat during a special election.

She later won a full term for the seat in November but was ousted in 2024 by Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska).

Democrats see a strong recruit in Peltola — a rare Democrat to win statewide in the traditionally Republican state. Still, the state’s red leanings and Sullivan’s incumbency will make it an uphill battle for the party.

The AARP was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research between Sept. 8-11, with 800 likely voters surveyed overall. The margin of error is 3.5 percentage points.

articles.body:
President Trump referred to surging gas prices as a small “price to pay” for the U.S. war in Iran while speaking to a crowd of supporters Wednesday in North Carolina.

“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done. Remember that. It’s a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more,” Trump said at a rally for GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley in Gastonia.

“But that’s going to come tumbling down,” he added, referring to gas prices. “That’s going to be like rocket ships in reverse.”

The comments came as fuel prices spiked as a result of the U.S. war in Iran.

The national average for regular unleaded gas jumped from $4.31 to $4.43 in the span of four days this week, according to AAA . Meanwhile, the national average for diesel jumped 42 cents over the last week.

Analysts raised concern over the price surge Thursday, noting uncertainty over the ongoing conflict.

“For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don’t have a baseline view,” Natasha Kaneva, a commodities strategist at JP Morgan, wrote to clients, according to Yahoo Finance.

“We simply don’t know how to model the endgame,” she said.

The Strait of Hormuz, the vital oil shipping lane, remains closed, playing a role in driving up energy prices.

In the U.S., Republicans are grappling with how to overcome Democrats’ affordability message as energy prices continue to rise.

Those costs could prove detrimental to Republicans in November as polls show Americans broadly disapproving of Trump’s handling of the economy.

A New York Times/Siena University poll released this week found that 62 percent of respondents said they disapproved of the way Trump was handling the economy, while only 36 percent said they approved.

articles.title: Kennedy Center director says closure will last 1 week ‘unless extended’
articles.summary: The Kennedy Center’s main building will be closed for at least a week for emergency repairs, its executive director said in court filings on Thursday, as the Department of Justice (DOJ) insists the move is unrelated to the Trump-aligned board’s decision to pursue long-term renovations. Executive Director Matt Floca wrote in a court declaration that…
articles.body:
The Kennedy Center’s main building will be closed for at least a week for emergency repairs, its executive director said in court filings on Thursday, as the Department of Justice (DOJ) insists the move is unrelated to the Trump-aligned board’s decision to pursue long-term renovations.

Executive Director Matt Floca wrote in a court declaration that he decided on Wednesday to temporarily cut off public access to the center after determining that there were “acute risks to public safety” due to structural damage in certain parts of the performing arts center.

“During this temporary closure, which will last for seven days, unless extended, I intend to assess existing safety risks to those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration,” he wrote, adding that a possible extension of that timeline would be evaluated on a weekly basis.

The filing cited a summer assessment of the roof terrace canopy conducted by an engineering firm and a recent water leak that caused a piece of ceiling plaster to collapse in the Grand Foyer as the immediate reasons for the closure.

An email sent to Kennedy Center staff members on Wednesday informing them of the plans also pointed to safety concerns with “soffit panels” and “electrical infrastructure.” It stated that nonessential employees should not report to the building.

The development comes as the Justice Department defended the closure as being independent from the board’s Tuesday vote , arguing that Floca’s decision complies with a federal judge’s previous order barring the Kennedy Center from shutting down for a prolonged period.

“No part of the Court’s preliminary injunction order forbids a temporary closure like this one,” DOJ lawyer Brantley Mayers wrote.

Fencing went up around the building on Wednesday, a day after President Trump’s handpicked board voted for a second time to close the center for repairs.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member challenging the closure and the board’s renewed attempts to add Trump’s name back to the facade, has asked U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper to hold an emergency hearing over the board’s latest vote.

“Closing the Kennedy Center without Judge Cooper’s approval appears to directly violate his order. This is an assault on the rule of law,” her attorneys Nathaniel Zelinsky and Norm Eisen said in a statement Wednesday. “The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper’s rulings whenever it suits them. In this country, no one — including the president — is above the law.”

Officials have described Trump as the “sole hope” for the Kennedy Center’s long-term survival, arguing that not putting his name on the building would hamper fundraising efforts as the institution faces “certain fiscal collapse.”

The president was spotted Wednesday night through an Air Force One window looking at a poster board with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH,” though the full image was not clear.

“I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close,” Trump told reporters Wednesday in Charlotte, N.C. “It’ll end up being ripped down.”

articles.title: Kennedy Center plaintiffs call for resignations or receivership
articles.summary: Eight historical, architectural and preservationist organizations that are plaintiffs in a case against the Kennedy Center on Thursday called for the performing arts center’s leaders to either resign or appoint a receiver. “If the current leadership of the Kennedy Center is unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty to protect the historic building and…
articles.body:
Eight historical, architectural and preservationist organizations that are plaintiffs in a case against the Kennedy Center on Thursday called for the performing arts center’s leaders to either resign or appoint a receiver.

“If the current leadership of the Kennedy Center is unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty to protect the historic building and the grounds of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the court should consider appointing a receiver or replacing that leadership,” the plaintiffs said in a statement provided by attorney Greg Werkheiser.

“The irrevocable loss of this iconic building — whether by intent, neglect or mismanagement — appears increasingly possible,” the statement continued. “The court has invited our coalition of eight nationally recognized architectural and preservation organizations to raise additional requests for relief if new facts appear to warrant judicial intervention. We are on the verge of such a moment.”

The plaintiffs comprise the American Institute of Architects, the American Society of Landscape Architects, the Committee of 100 on the Federal City, the DC Preservation League, Docomomo US, the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the Society of Architectural Historians and the Cultural Landscape Foundation.

Werkheiser, whose law firm, Cultural Heritage Partners, is one of three firms representing the organizations, told reporters they will “likely soon” file for receivership.

“We feel an obligation, no matter how realistic we think it is, to first publicly and clearly call, one last time, on the trustees to particularly focus on their legal fiduciary duties,” he said.

He later said that requesting a receivership for the Kennedy Center does not require it to go into bankruptcy.

“But circumstances are changing rapidly,” he warned. “In requiring independent protection, the court could consider measures to put someone else, not someone that we pick, not someone that the government picks, but someone that the court picks and vets –– put them in charge of preserving the historic building.”

Werkheiser also said the plaintiffs were “paying close attention” to photos shared as part of a court filing from Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who challenged the Trump administration in a separate lawsuit, showing President Trump aboard Air Force One reading a placard that read “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

“My mom didn’t raise the smartest person, but I know, always, that we have to wait for verification of those things before we can really express any strong opinion,” Werkheiser said.

The Hill has reached out to the Kennedy Center and the White House for comment.

Werkheiser emphasized that Congress has $257 million set aside for repairs to the venue, prompting the center’s Trump-aligned board to pursue long-term renovations. He added that Trump can lead the renovations and financially rescue the center.

“But on Tuesday, [U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper] again held that the board cannot place President Trump’s name on the Kennedy Center building [and] were grounds without congressional authorization, which, of course, he currently lacks,” the attorney said. “President Trump then said that he will withhold the renovations funded by Congress and the American people unless that ruling is overturned and he will refuse to raise additional funds.”

Werkheiser said Trump has the “extraordinary responsibility” to use his power to keep the center running, “not extraordinary leverage to demand the institution honor him.”

He later noted that board members have an “affirmative duty” to preserve the Kennedy Center as a performing arts center and living memorial to former President John F. Kennedy.

“Judge Cooper’s been very clear about that,” Werkheiser continued. “He said the trustees aren’t mere figureheads. They are duty-bound to fulfill their roles with due care and some modicum of independence, especially when they’re managing property held in trust for the American people.”

The center’s main building will be closed for at least a week for emergency repairs. Executive Director Matt Floca wrote in a court declaration that the decision to close the building was due to “acute risks to public safety” from structural damage in some areas of the arts center.

The Department of Justice defended the closure and said Floca’s decision is in line with a federal judge’s prior order preventing the center from being closed for a prolonged period.

Fencing was set up around the building on Wednesday after the board voted for a second time to shut the center down for repairs.

articles.title: The cameras are already everywhere, but no one wrote the rules
articles.summary: No federal legislative framework governs law enforcement’s use of these systems.
articles.body:
I spent 20 years in law enforcement. I commanded the Investigative Services Division, worked narcotics and served on the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force with the FBI and DEA.

I’ll begin where my fellow skeptics usually will not: an automated license plate reader is a good tool. It does quickly what detectives once did slowly or never manage to do at all. It places a specific vehicle at a specific place at a specific time, and has recovered stolen cars, located missing children and put shooters in handcuffs.

The tool is not the problem. The absence of any national rule governing it is.

In September, the Congressional Research Service stated the situation plainly . No federal legislative framework governs law enforcement’s use of these systems. Instead, a patchwork of state law and agency policy exists.

Meanwhile, the network kept growing. More than 120,000 Flock Safety cameras now operate across 49 states , feeding thousands of agencies who search one another’s data across jurisdictional lines . The only federal constraint is the Fourth Amendment, which courts interpret one case at a time, and so far, they have declined to extend the warrant requirement to plate reader data .

In August, Flock Safety announced it would cut its recommended retention period from 30 days to seven, give agencies tighter control over cross-agency sharing, require officers to tie every search to a case code and automatically flag abnormal query patterns for review. Those are genuine improvements. As a commander, I would have welcomed every one of them.

They are also corporate policy, revocable by the same corporation, adopted after abuses were documented rather than before. A policy is a promise. A law is an obligation. The difference matters only when someone wants to break it, which is precisely when it matters most.

And people have broken it. An officer in Milwaukee ran a woman he had been involved with through the system scores of times. An audit in Dayton surfaced thousands of searches whose stated purpose did not match their apparent use. Illinois regulators found data flowing to federal immigration authorities through a channel that state law did not permit.

Not one of those incidents required a hacker or a warrant. Each required only a login and a bad reason.

States noticed. California, Virginia, Illinois, Maine and New Hampshire now fix retention periods and restrict sharing by statute. Washington lawmakers opened with a 72-hour limit and settled on 21 days after police reasonably objected . Redmond Police Chief Darrell Lowe told a hearing that three days offers no investigative value and only masquerades as privacy . In Pennsylvania, a bipartisan group has proposed rules covering access, documented search justification, audit trails, retention, transparency, civil penalties and a private right of action for people harmed by misuse.

It is good work but none of it solves the actual problem. A driver’s protections now change at a state line on a network which does not recognize state lines. We have built a national system and governed it locally, which is another way of saying we have not governed it.

A federal standard does not require reinventing anything. Five elements would cover it.

Set a uniform retention ceiling, with a documented preservation exception tied to an open case number. Require every query to log a named user, a case number and a stated offense, in a record open to audit. Require federal agencies to obtain a warrant before querying state and local databases, closing the loophole letting Washington buy or borrow what it cannot lawfully compel. Prohibit outright the use of this network for immigration enforcement or for tracking anyone who crossed a state line for lawful medical care. And give the standard teeth, through civil liability and suppression, because a rule carrying no consequence is a suggestion.

Congress already has the pieces on the table. Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) introduced the PRIVACY Act , which would require a federal warrant before querying state and local plate reader systems and limit retention of unrelated data.

Reps. Scott Perry (R-Pa.) and Chuy Garcia (D-Ill.) have drafted an amendment barring recipients of federal highway funding from using these cameras for anything except tolling. I would not vote for the second one. It throws out a working tool to solve a governance failure. But its existence tells you how far the frustration now runs, and how strange the coalition has become.

Some will argue any of this ties the hands of good cops. I was one for two decades, and I will tell you what actually ties our hands: a defense attorney holding an audit log showing officers in the same system ran searches nobody can justify. Transparency does not weaken an investigation. It is what lets the investigation survive cross-examination.

These cameras do not watch for criminals. They watch everyone and sort it out afterward. That may still be a bargain worth making. But a country should make a bargain like this one on purpose, in daylight, under rules written by people answerable to voters, not inherit it by procurement while nobody was paying attention.

Joe Broadmeadow is a retired police captain who commanded the Investigative Services Division, worked narcotics, and served on the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force with the FBI and DEA. He is an author and the founder of JEBWizard Publishing.
