articles.body:
President Trump was seen on Air Force One looking at a placard that appears to depict the potential demolition of the Kennedy Center amid an ongoing legal battle over getting his name on the building and starting renovations.

Zoomed-in photos taken by Agence France-Presse photojournalist Brendan Smialowski Wednesday night showed Trump viewing the board through the plane’s windows after landing at Joint Base Andrews.

The photos come as the Kennedy Center board voted to close the main building and Trump made the planned renovations contingent on his name being put on the building.

Trump told reporters Wednesday after arriving in North Carolina that the center is a “mess” and that the administration deserves recognition if it fixes it up.

“So, for the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close,” he said. “It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.”

The president and the board have said the closure is needed to do some much-needed repairs. Administration officials have posted videos of a piece of ceiling collapsing.

Fencing also went up around the main building Wednesday.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the board, called for an emergency hearing to explain the closure.

But court orders have blocked the closure of the building and the addition of Trump’s name. The center’s director and the White House have said the building will be closed for one week.

In a filing submitted Thursday morning, the board said the closure was decided because of “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration at the Center.”

Resolutions from the board have pointed to Trump’s fundraising skills as the only way to save the building.

Trump has also said he’s put in $17 million in donations to “keep it afloat.”

He said in a Truth Social post Tuesday that the renovations won’t begin until the court approves the board’s plan to put his name on the building.

articles.title: Judge gives Blanche deadline, warns of possible contempt charges over Epstein files
articles.summary: A federal judge gave Attorney General Todd Blanche a deadline to comply with court orders Wednesday regarding the release of certain information in the Epstein files, threatening contempt charges for failure to comply. U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan stated in a Wednesday opinion that Blanche and his office were not following court orders concerning redactions…
articles.body:
A federal judge gave Attorney General Todd Blanche a deadline to comply with court orders Wednesday regarding the release of certain information in the Epstein files, threatening contempt charges for failure to comply.

U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan stated in a Wednesday opinion that Blanche and his office were not following court orders concerning redactions in requested documentation related to the activities of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell.

He gave the Department of Justice (DOJ) until Sept. 24 to provide the records or explain to the court why its orders were not “clear and unambiguous” — finding the attorney general’s argument against the records’ release to be “without merit.”

Sullivan noted in his opinion that “a civil contempt finding at this juncture would be premature” but did not rule out the possibility if the deadline is not met.

The lawsuit was filed by attorney and independent journalist Katie Phang, who alleged that the DOJ has violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA) by withholding information.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward argued in July that the redactions in the files were allowed under the law as they contained the names of victims and private email addresses.

“One of the complicating aspects of administering the EFTA is that many communications written by victims, without context, can appear disturbing on their face,” Woodward wrote. “Consistent with that statutory authority, the Department has sought to prevent victim PII from becoming public even in instances where the victims eventually became complicit or engaged in reprehensible activity or communications.”

The court sided against the DOJ and ordered Blanche to “support his representation that the following redactions are the names of victims” — including correspondences with Epstein in files EFTA01187999 , EFTA02504630 and EFTA01022356 .

The ruling requires Blanche to release handwritten FBI interview notes and foreign language materials.

The DOJ argued that it could not release these files because “it was not practicable for a first-level reviewer to determine the responsiveness of a foreign language document,” which the court sided against.

“There are redactions that my lawsuit obviously says are illegal redactions or illegal withholdings,” Phang said in a video posted Wednesday.

“I can’t imagine that anybody would be satisfied that there’s still millions of documents that Todd Blanche says are duplicative or nonresponsive, and he won’t even turn them over to the people,” she continued.

articles.title: Will procedural votes cost 2 House Democrats their committee assignments?
articles.summary: Democratic Reps. Jared Golden and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faced criticism from party leadership after voting with Republicans to pass a special rule on Sept. 1.
articles.body:
On Sept. 1, two Democrats, Reps. Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) had the audacity to vote in favor of a special rule without first informing their leaders of their intentions.

The top three House Democratic leaders — Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Whip Katherine Clark (Mass.), and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (Calif.), were enraged and issued a terse joint statement : “The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust.” The statement concluded that the action “necessitates a serious response,” and called on the caucus’s Committee on Caucus Rules “to take this up in short order.”

What caused such a brouhaha over a vote on a simple procedural resolution? Ordinarily, such rules providing for the consideration of legislation are adopted along strict party-line votes, the exceptions more recently being a handful of Republicans who stray from the pack on rule votes. In this instance, however, the rule was narrowly adopted, 210-208, with the votes of the two Democrats providing the winning margin for Republicans.

Moreover, one of the measures the special rule made in order was a simple House resolution clearly designed to put House Democrats in an embarrassing box. It read, “Resolved, that the House of Representatives condemns and denounces socialism in all its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America, and opposes the implementation of socialist policies in the United States.”

With democratic socialist movement candidates winning surprising election victories in several states, including Democratic primaries, more moderate Democrats have been fumbling for ways to differentiate themselves from the taint of socialism.

Both offending members are moderates. Gluesenkamp Perez, in her second term, is co-chair of the Democratic Party’s centrist Blue Dog Coalition. Golden, a fourth termer, is retiring at the end of this Congress , but was lured by the inclusion in the same special rule of a bill titled, “The Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act” — a crustacean near and dear to his fellow Mainers.

As of this writing, the Democratic caucus rules committee had still not come forward with a recommendation on how to deal with the two defectors. There was considerable talk among angry colleagues, however, about stripping them of their committee assignments. For Golden, who serves on the Armed Services and Natural Resources committees, that would not be a major setback, since he’s retiring next January. For Gluesenkamp Perez, on the other hand, it would be a major blow, as her sole committee assignment is on the prestigious and powerful House Appropriations Committee.

What is curious, though, is why the disciplinary ball has been tossed into the court of the 13-member caucus rules committee chaired by Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.). Its sole responsibility (until now), has been to recommend codifications and revisions of the caucus rules, “as circumstances may indicate, and, if necessary, recommend action to the caucus.”

Ordinarily, committee membership issues are handled by the Democratic Steering and Policy Committee, chaired by the Speaker (or, when in the minority, the party leader). Among other things, the committee “is vested with the authority to recommend vacating committee chairs and removing members from committees by majority vote, subject then to a final vote by the full caucus.” Even if the caucus recommends removal of a member, that decision must be finalized by a vote of the full House which elects (and de-selects) all committees and their members.

It may be that the leadership already has some lesser form of admonishment in mind, such as a reprimand. After all, there is no current caucus rule barring members from voting against their party’s wishes. How can you punish someone for violating a rule that doesn’t exist? It is unlikely the caucus rules committee will attempt simultaneously to propose and then enforce such a rule retroactively.

There was a time when House Democrats had a rule that empowered their caucus, by a two-thirds vote, to bind members’ floor votes on specified legislation. That was later repealed as the party became more diverse and charges against abuses of “King Caucus” began to bite back.

I suspect this episode will not result in removing the two defectors from their committees. Instead, it will more likely result in a new rule (or at least an informal one), advising Democratic members to inform their leadership in advance of their intention to vote against the party’s stated position on designated matters.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

articles.title: Jeffries punts on possible punishment for Dem defectors
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is staying mum on the thorny question of whether Democratic defectors should face repercussions. “I’ll have more to say … about the situation when we have more to say about the situation,” Jeffries told reporters Thursday in the Capitol. A pair of centrist Democrats — Reps. Jared Golden (Maine)…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is staying mum on the thorny question of whether Democratic defectors should face repercussions.

“I’ll have more to say … about the situation when we have more to say about the situation,” Jeffries told reporters Thursday in the Capitol.

A pair of centrist Democrats — Reps. Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) — have crossed the aisle on two occasions in recent weeks to help rescue the Republicans’ legislative agenda heading into the midterm elections.

The votes have infuriated Democratic leaders and rank-and-file members, who have centered their campaign message on affordability and were frustrated that members of their own party helped to bring other topics to the floor that might hurt battleground Democrats at the polls.

Some of those lawmakers want to strip Gluesenkamp Perez of a plum committee assignment on the Appropriations panel, while Golden is facing less scrutiny because he’s retiring at the end of this term.

The defections have been a headache for Jeffries and his leadership team, who like their chances of flipping the House but want to keep the focus on the high cost of living under President Trump’s second term. GOP leaders have sought to change the subject by focusing on legislation that highlights the Democrats’ vulnerabilities, and twice this month Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez have helped them in that effort.

In the first episode, the two centrists backed a Republican rule to help bring a final vote on legislation that helps lobstermen. Their decision also ensured votes on GOP proposals to condemn socialism, roll back environmental protections and bar U.S. universities from participating in boycotts of Israel — all hot-button issues Republicans see as beneficial on the campaign trail.

The second occasion came Tuesday, when the pair crossed the aisle again to ensure a vote on a Russian sanctions bill, which divided Democrats and was rejected by party leaders because it gave Trump new tariff authorities.

After the first instance, Jeffries called a special meeting of the Democrats’ Committee on Caucus Rules to examine potential changes to the party’s internal rules heading into the next Congress. But the House left Washington on Wednesday with no decisions made.

“The process will play out,” Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), a member of the committee, said Wednesday.

Democratic leaders are facing pressure to crack the whip, if only to send a message to incoming Democrats that defections on rule votes won’t be tolerated in the next Congress. It’s clear, however, that no announcements will be coming before the elections, as Jeffries and his leadership team are eager to shelve the defection scandal and direct their message on the volatile economy.

“We’ll address the situation when we address the situation,” Jeffries said Thursday. “We’re focused right now on taking back control of the House of Representatives. That’s what the American people want to see: a dramatic change in this country, because they are drowning.”

articles.title: Jon Kyl, 3-term Arizona senator, dies at 84
articles.summary: Former Sen. Jon Kyl (R-Ariz.), who served in Congress for more than 25 years, died at 84 years old from complications related to a neurological disease, his family announced Thursday. “Our husband, father, grandfather, son, and brother, Jon Kyl, has passed away at the age of 84 due to complications from a neurological disease,” a…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Jon Kyl (R-Ariz.), who served in Congress for more than 25 years, died at 84 years old from complications related to a neurological disease, his family announced Thursday.

“Our husband, father, grandfather, son, and brother, Jon Kyl, has passed away at the age of 84 due to complications from a neurological disease,” a statement from Kyl’s family reads.

“We know that Jon belonged to all of Arizona, a state he loved and explored with vigor, curiosity, and wonder. Serving his state and nation in Congress was a privilege and responsibility he honored and respected. We are grateful for his full and meaningful public life.”

“We are grateful, too, for his full and meaningful family life, guided by his faith and endowed with honor, warmth, and love. We cherish his presence in our lives and are thankful he has joined his beloved Creator, Jesus Christ,” the statement concluded.

Memorial services for Kyl will be announced later.

The former GOP lawmaker announced he was diagnosed with dementia in late 2025 and said he would be withdrawing from public life at the time.

He served the Grand Canyon State in the House from 1987-95 before joining the Senate from 1995 to 2013, rising to minority whip during his final years in office. Kyl was appointed by former Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey (R) to fill the seat vacated by the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) in 2018 for the remaining months of McCain’s term.

Between his Senate stints, Kyl worked as a lobbyist, notably guiding Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination through the upper chamber.

He also lobbied on behalf of young immigrants brought to the U.S. illegally as children, following President Trump’s decision to end the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program during his first term.

“Jon Kyl gave Arizona nearly three decades of principled, thoughtful leadership — and he gave me something just as valuable: his mentorship and friendship. I’ll miss him deeply. Rest in peace, Senator Kyl,” Ducey wrote on social media .

Kyl was married for more than 50 years to his wife, Caryll, with whom he shared two children, Kristine and John, and four grandchildren.

The couple met during Kyl’s time in college; Caryll worked as a nurse to put Kyl through law school. He graduated from law school in 1966 and moved to Phoenix to pursue his law career.

articles.title: President Trump is bringing healthy food from harvest to hallways
articles.summary: The Trump administration is launching initiatives to improve school nutrition by increasing farm-to-school grant funding and investing in cafeteria equipment upgrades.
articles.body:
As a new school year kicks into gear, the Trump administration is celebrating the start of a new era of school nutrition — one that will bring even more real food from America’s farms into school cafeterias.

America’s schools are vital partners in helping children receive the nutrients they need for their learning and development. And for many students, schools are where they get most of their meals and the healthiest food they eat all day. Each school day, the National School Lunch Program serves about 30 million students, while the School Breakfast Program serves approximately 15 million. That’s over 4.8 billion lunches and 2.5 billion breakfasts a year — making schools one of the few places where we can consistently influence lifelong eating habits.

Through these programs, many schools are already providing students with whole, nutrient-dense food, which feature prominently in the 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans we released earlier this year. The message is simple: eat real food. By aligning school meals with these evidence-based recommendations, schools use the healthy food made by America’s farmers and ranchers to help solve our national chronic disease epidemic.

To facilitate this alignment, the U.S. Department of Agriculture is working to finalize a proposed school meals rule, which will ensure the Dietary Guidelines are reflected on breakfast and lunch trays in schools across America. Among other MAHA-inspired solutions, the rule will promote whole food breakfast options, healthy cooking methods, 100 percent whole grains, whole fruit and whole milk. Without a doubt, this will be the most transformative action we have taken to date for our children, and for the future of America.

The next step in our mission to Make America Healthy Again is to get even more of the great bounty of America’s harvest into America’s schools. For the upcoming school year, USDA is providing up to $25 million in additional Patrick Leahy Farm to School Grant Program funding, which leverages the healthy food grown by our farmers and ranchers to support local communities. The department already awarded two cohorts a total of $20 million in April 2026 — the largest investment in the history of the program. One recipient of that funding was the Pennsylvania Beef Council, which is partnering with 175 local schools across the Keystone State to serve nearly 300,000 students, who will now enjoy a delicious source of protein in their school cafeteria, right from their own backyard.

In practice, the concept of “farm to table” — or in this case, “harvest to hallways” — also involves a few intermediary steps. Once healthy local food arrives in the school kitchen, it needs to be stored, cooked and served. Unfortunately, much of the basic infrastructure this requires is sorely out of date, if not altogether absent in some locations. That’s why USDA is stepping up to invest up to $70 million for schools to use in upgrading cafeteria cold storage, stoves and other equipment. This includes $20 million in National School Lunch Program Assistance Grants awarded to states this month, giving schools across America access to the equipment they need to prepare more meals from scratch.

Thanks to President Trump’s unprecedented leadership, our effort to make school meals healthier is also attracting support from the private sector. For example, Tyson Foods is committing $1 million over the next two years to strengthen childhood access to food and nutrition resources, especially in rural communities. Sysco and Aramark have also pledged support, including through school district partnerships, nutrition education and menu development services. We are also working to secure partnerships from other companies, as this investing in the health of our nation is truly a team effort.

At the end of the day, putting America First means putting America’s children first. A healthier future is within reach, but only if we lean into the nutritious food grown by America’s farmers, ranchers and producers. By connecting that food with schools across America, we are investing in the health of the next generation, one child at a time.

Brooke L. Rollins is U.S. secretary of Agriculture and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services.

articles.title: Florida Republican breaks with Trump on immigration in campaign ad: Latino voters ‘feel betrayed’
articles.summary: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) accused President Trump of going “too far” with federal immigration enforcement operations in a campaign advertisement released Thursday. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” said Salazar, who’s running for reelection in November, in the new clip. “You can be for immigration…
articles.body:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) accused President Trump of going “too far” with federal immigration enforcement operations in a campaign advertisement released Thursday.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” said Salazar, who’s running for reelection in November, in the new clip .

“You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism,” the Republican continued. “I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

The ad, which will run on TV and online in South Florida, is one of the first of several new political ads the Republican’s campaign team plans to share ahead of the midterms, according to a Thursday press release .

The comment marks a notable break from a Trump-endorsed Republican amid her reelection bid in Florida. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, previously shifted its rating in this race from “solidly Republican” to “likely Republican.”

The president backed Salazar in a February Truth Social post, praising the former news anchor’s “Wisdom and Courage” in confronting “the Corrupt Fake News.”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Salazar is running against Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez in the state’s 27th Congressional District, a seat she was first elected to in 2020. The district, which includes parts of Miami, is home to one of the highest foreign-born populations of any House district.

On Monday, Salazar spoke out following reports that immigration agents had detained Luis Galeano, an exiled Venezuelan journalist, in Miami.

The Venezuelan government stripped Galeano’s citizenship due to his criticism of the regime, and his U.S. asylum application has been pending for seven years.

“I have been clear with the Administration: enforce the law and deport dangerous individuals, but do not treat political exiles like criminals,” Salazar said in a statement shared on social media. “We are still learning the details of his detention, but his case must be reviewed immediately and with the full weight of what he has already endured.”

Last year, Salazar introduced the Dignity Act , a bipartisan immigration bill that has divided House Republicans. The legislation would allow migrants who arrived in the country without proper documentation before 2021 and do not have criminal records to gain new legal status if they pay $7,000 in restitution as well as any owed back taxes.

Salazar has emphasized the bill would not provide this population with a path to citizenship, saying it is not “amnesty.”

Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, has also criticized the Trump administration over its immigration enforcement operations, and he referenced his familial background in similar attack ads against Trump.

“This community is built by hard-working immigrants just like them,” Rodriguez said in a January campaign ad . “Yes, secure borders matter, but so does due process and our constitution. When our leaders stay silent as these rights are trampled on, that silence is not leadership.”

articles.body:
It’s Thursday, and National Pawpaw Day. Had to look that one up … apparently, it has a creamy banana-mango flavor. Hm.

(Editor’s note: Rhoda in Top Chef Season 23 made an amazing dish with pawpaws.)

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com or awalker@thehill.com .

Talarico vs. Paxton; El-Sayed vs. Rogers

OpenAI on Wednesday shared six “ misalignment examples ” of its artificial intelligence going rogue.

The models (separately) self-generated instructions, added instructions to conceal mistakes, fabricated information, uploaded files to the internet without permission, used internal software for unsanctioned communication, and shared files between collaborating agents.

“These are reports of individual instances and shouldn’t be considered reflective of how often misalignment occurs across our models,” OpenAI assured readers in a blog post.

💡 Why this matters: It’s been a big week for freaking out about AI. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , xAI CEO Elon Musk and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently rallied for a development slowdown.

The calls came after former OpenAI and Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said researchers at the firms “believe AI could kill all humans” but still push forward in a race to develop superintelligence on the social platform X.

What next?: OpenAI plans to create a new framework to track and investigate incidents like this.

The House went back on recess after Wednesday, despite calls from Democrats to work on legislation for AI safeguards. They’ll be back after the November midterm elections.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) requested to pass legislation on Wednesday to require tech companies to have a “kill switch” for superintelligent AI. It was blocked by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.)

Amodei’s call for AI companies to have an antitrust waiver in his Saturday blog post isn’t going over great in Washington.

“There is absolutely no world in which I will consent to giving the most powerful companies in the history of the world — a small group of three or four of them — antitrust exemptions so they can what … collude together? Absolutely no way that’s happening,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing with FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) echoed Hawley. “To watch AI CEOs saying, ‘We’re about to destroy the world, so give us control of the government so we can lock in our monopoly status and prevent any innovation from challenging us,’ is just lunacy.”

Hasan Piker appeared on “The Axios Show” for an interview released Thursday , as Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed seeks distance from the leftwing Twitch streamer who previously campaigned with him.

When prompted by Axios’s Alex Thompson about his past comments, Piker affirmed his belief that U.S. is the “top dog of terrorism.”

Thompson asked if the streamer still felt America was worse than al-Qaeda, to which Piker responded, “pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes.”

“If you’re killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror,” Piker later added. “This doesn’t mean that all Americans are terrorists, but the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again.”

El-Sayed’s response to Axios: “I do not agree with this statement [on al-Qaeda], nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer.”

However, El-Sayed has refused calls to disavow Piker entirely.

“The reason I talk to Hasan isn’t because of Hasan, it’s because of the 3 million people who pay attention to what he has to say,” El-Sayed said Tuesday night at a debate that Rogers declined to join.

TLDR: the Senate races in Michigan and Texas are really, really close.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and state Sen. James Talarico are deadlocked 47 days until election day.

The Hill/Emerson College Polling found in their survey that 47 percent of Texas voters backed Talarico compared to Paxton’s 46 percent.

Other recent polls have put Talarico slightly ahead.

A Telemundo/Mason-Dixon Polling & Research survey published Tuesday gave Talarico a three-point lead . Two June surveys from Sienna University had the candidates tied, but by the end of July, Talarico held a four-point lead.

The new survey also asked respondents their opinions on the GOP’s midterm convention hosted earlier this month. Of those who were aware of the convention, 53 percent of Democrats and 59 percent of Republicans said the event heightened their excitement to cast ballots in November.

Texas voters ranked the economy as their top priority, with 36 percent placing it higher than other issues like immigration and healthcare.

A new poll puts Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed slightly ahead of former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

Of the respondents to The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey, 48 percent supported El-Sayed, and 46 percent backed Rogers.

Spencer Kimball, the executive director of Emerson College Polling, pointed to educational background as a significant divide between voters.

“Voters without a four-year degree favor Rogers, 48 percent to 45 percent, while college graduates support El-Sayed, 53 percent to 42 percent,” he said.

The Senate race is one of seven that the Cook Political Report labels a “toss-up.”

No show: Both candidates were supposed to appear for a Tuesday debate. Rogers, however, pulled out , citing “media bias.”

Rogers’s communications director called out moderator, Roop Raj, in a statement, writing that “Roop Raj has made his position clear, from praising Abdul as ‘brilliant,’ to being celebrated by Hasan Piker as ‘my GOAT,’ and bragging about his political stunts.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s Wednesday comments welcoming Canada to join the European Union (EU) as an “associate member” has stirred up trouble across the pond.

President Trump in response threated tariffs against the EU and labeled Canada’s potential joining a “hostile act.”

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe,” Trump told reporters Wednesday.

He’ll consider it: On Thursday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to the European Parliament and said, “A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies. An alliance not defined by what we oppose but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability.”

“We welcome this ambition,” he said, after name-checking the idea of von der Leyen, who was sitting in the audience. “Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties.”

Carney added that an “overwhelming majority” of Canadians support closer ties with Europe. But he didn’t give a clear endorsement of the associate member idea, saying, “We welcome this ambition.”

“We hold common values, for which we have always fought and for whose defense we must always remain vigilant,” Carney told the European Parliament.

The Kennedy Center’s main building will be closed for at least a week for emergency repairs, its executive director said in court filings on Thursday, as the Justice Department insists that move is unrelated to the Trump-aligned board’s decision to pursue long-term renovations.

articles.title: Patrick Clancy says he leans on his children for support
articles.summary: Patrick Clancy’s testimony led to online speculation and conspiracies that he had a role in his children’s deaths.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Patrick Clancy has spoken out publicly for the first time since he took the stand seven weeks ago in his ex-wife Lindsey Clancy’s murder trial.

In an interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes,” Clancy told the outlet he leans on his children for support.

“I talk to them,” he said in a promo posted to social platform X .

“What do you say to them?” correspondent Ross Douthat asked.

“‘Help me,'” Clancy responded. “All the time.”

Lindsay Clancy was charged with the murder of her three children in 2023. In his testimony, the ex-husband spoke of the mother’s declining mental health in the months leading up to the killings — including how she struggled with paranoia, suicidal thoughts, insomnia, depression and intrusive thoughts; and about harming the children.

His testimony was the first to be used by the prosecution, who argued Lindsay Clancy was sane when she killed her children and that it was premeditated. The defense made the case she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and, therefore, could not be held criminally responsible.

Clancy’s testimony led to online speculation and conspiracies that he played a role in his children’s deaths. He told “60 Minutes” that the baseless theories are deeply harmful to the legacy of his children and a distraction to perinatal health.

The case ultimately ended in a mistrial after seven days of deliberation, with one lone juror refusing to find the mother not criminally responsible. Clancy has now retained attorney Martin G. Weinberg, who was a part of Karen Read’s legal team, and will appear in court again at the end of September.

It is not yet known whether prosecutors will seek to retry her.

The “60 Minutes” episode will air Sunday, Sept. 20 at 7 p.m. Eastern time.

articles.title: Judge restricts immigration officers from making warrantless arrests in Southern California
articles.summary: A federal judge on Wednesday barred immigration enforcement officers from making arrests without a warrant in Southern California. U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong granted a preliminary injunction on Sept. 2, which was unsealed on Wednesday. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Southern California, in partnership with nonprofit public interest law firm Public Counsel…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Wednesday barred immigration enforcement officers from making arrests without a warrant in Southern California.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong granted a preliminary injunction on Sept. 2, which was unsealed on Wednesday. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Southern California, in partnership with nonprofit public interest law firm Public Counsel and several Los Angeles immigrant advocacy groups, filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) last year after the region saw a massive surge in immigration enforcement.

The preliminary injunction came from the Central District of California, which covers Los Angeles, Orange, San Bernardino, Ventura and San Luis Obispo counties.

Frimpong — appointed by former President Biden — ordered the federal government to thoroughly document the probable causes that lead to arrests before obtaining a warrant, in order to prove the arrests were “proper.” She added that the plaintiffs have shown that the policy has been ongoing, pointing to DHS officer testimony.

“And the ensuing detention (that would stem from an unlawful arrest) naturally constitutes irreparable harm,” Frimpong wrote. “Defendants’ arguments to the contrary do not persuade this Court otherwise.”

The order requires officers not to rely on the “escape risk” standard set forth by Todd Lyons, former acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which suggested that being an undocumented immigrant was sufficient as a likelihood of escape.

The Hill has reached out to DHS for comment.

The Supreme Court lifted a previous temporary restraining order issued by Frimpong last September. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, President Trump’s second appointee to the court, indicated that the plaintiffs likely had no legal right to sue.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) praised Frimpong’s order, saying Trump has “tested” the City of Angels “time and time again, and we have stood strong.”

“For more than a year, families across our city have lived with the fear that a trip to work, a walk down the street, or a goodbye in the morning could end with a loved one being taken away,” Bass said in a statement. “Today’s ruling is an important protection against the warrantless arrests that have racially targeted Angelenos and terrorized communities.”

Mayra Joachin, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Southern California, called the ruling one of the most important decisions “in the community’s effort to end the federal government’s cruel and illegal practice of abducting people and separating them from their families.”

Judges in Oregon, Colorado, Washington, D.C., and the Eastern District of California have issued similar orders in the past year, as the Trump administration continues to pursue its sweeping immigration crackdown.

Frimpong previously held DHS in contempt after the department delayed in complying with an order to release digital copies of communications on the cellphones of more than 800 immigration agents. Plaintiffs alleged that officers used racial slurs in those communications and argued that access to cellphone data would provide evidence to support their claims.

articles.title: Senate bill on carbon dioxide wells threatens rural water supplies
articles.summary: A new section of the Water Resources Development Act of 2026 proposes groundwater protection exemptions for carbon dioxide injection wells that critics argue will threaten the livelihoods of rural farmers and ranchers.
articles.body:
The U.S. Senate is considering legislation that will weaken groundwater protections, pertaining to wells engineered for long-term storage of carbon dioxide.

The language in question is buried in the last section of a larger water resources package, titled “Non-potable Aquifer Exemption for Class VI Wells” from the Water Resources Development Act of 2026 . This section would direct EPA “to provide for exemptions that allow the use of non-potable aquifers for Class VI wells.”

There are two exemptions in the bill. One applies if “the aquifer, or portion of the aquifer, does not currently serve as a source of drinking water” and “cannot now and will not in the future serve as a source of drinking water.” The other applies if “the total dissolved solids content of the ground water from the aquifer, or portion of the aquifer,” is between 3 and 10 grams per liter, and “the aquifer, or portion of the aquifer, is not reasonably expected to supply a public water system.”

That may sound complex, but here’s the reality: These two exemptions would discriminate against small rural communities and especially harm rural ranchers and farmers, because they could exempt irrigation water and water used for livestock watering operations. The problem is that just because people aren’t drinking or aren’t expected to drink the water, it follows that its content is irrelevant.

In addition, the exemptions would allow these carbon dioxide wells to be situated beneath or near aquifers that, while not being used currently for drinking water by people, could be in the future given the availability of reverse osmosis and other emerging water treatment technologies.

If a Class VI well were to leak carbon dioxide into an aquifer used for irrigation and livestock, it would acidify the water and mobilize heavy metals and potentially other toxic materials rendering it unusable in agriculture or for any drinking water purposes now or in the future.

Well documented well failures at injection wells in Illinois and Texas have shown that carbon capture injection wells need more stringent protections, not less.

This legislation would have had a direct impact on a proposed project in Montana, exempting certain aquifers from review when EPA considers Class VI well permits. The Snowy River Carbon Sequestration Project was a proposed ExxonMobil (via Denbury Carbon Solutions) facility in southeastern Montana’s Carter County designed to inject 150 million tons of carbon dioxide underground over 20 years. The carbon dioxide was to be primarily sourced from Wyoming gas plants and sequestered via up to 15 wells.

Landowners, including farmers and ranchers, were opposed because they saw no meaningful economic benefit but rather threats to range land and livelihoods, including degradation of surface and groundwater resources. The EPA found the Bureau of Land Management environmental assessment of potential impacts on groundwater aquifers inadequate. These included several shallow alluvial plain aquifers and a deeper sandstone aquifer. The shallower aquifers were primarily used for watering livestock, although they did qualify as underground sources of drinking water.

Facing heavy local and environmental scrutiny over agricultural disruption, groundwater threats, and pipeline safety, the bureau scaled back its review. Instead of approving the entire project footprint, the agency authorized only a single stratigraphic test well on state land to collect geologic and hydrologic data. Recently, Exxon removed the permit application , in large part due to the massive local opposition. However, projects like this one have a greater chance of moving forward if the law is changed to permit these carbon dioxide wells to be sited near aquifers used for rural wells and watering livestock.

This bill, exempting aquifers not currently used for drinking water (by people), imperils the livelihoods of small rural communities dependent on ranching and farming. It should be stopped.

Ted Schettler is science director at the Science and Environmental Health Network . Liz Barbour is a southeastern Montana rancher, rural advocate, and community organizer who led local opposition to the proposed Snowy River Carbon Sequestration Project.

articles.title: Hasan Piker says ‘pound for pound’ US commits more terrorism than al-Qaeda
articles.summary: Progressive pundit Hasan Piker argued that the U.S. commits more terrorism around the world than the Islamic terrorist group al-Qaeda, comments that are sparking backlash from both Republicans and Democrats. “You once said that America is the top dog in terrorism. Do you think American then is worse than al-Qaeda?” journalist Alex Thompson asked Piker…
articles.body:
Progressive pundit Hasan Piker argued that the U.S. commits more terrorism around the world than the Islamic terrorist group al-Qaeda , comments that are sparking backlash from both Republicans and Democrats.

“You once said that America is the top dog in terrorism. Do you think American then is worse than al-Qaeda?” journalist Alex Thompson asked Piker during a recent appearance on “The Axios Show.”

“Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes,” Piker responded. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.”

The U.S. government is waging terror “not only on regular civilians,” the pundit continued, “but it’s also having consequences on ourselves.”

“One clear example of this is what we did in Minab,” he said, referring to the bombing of a school in Iran earlier this year, which was believed to have been hit by U.S. weapons, but the Pentagon has not taken responsibility for.

“If you’re killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror,” Piker continued. “That doesn’t mean that all Americans are terrorists, but the reality is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again.”

The backlash to his comments has been swift online.

“Comparing America to al-Qaeda wasn’t an accident — Piker has built a brand on anti-American hate,” Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) wrote on social platform X. “This is a man who said America “deserved” 9/11, who framed a newspaper with the Twin Towers on it for his backdrop, and who has spent years excusing the very terrorists who’ve targeted our country. That’s not edgy commentary.”

The official Republicans X account posted the clip and wrote “every single Democrat who is supported by this garbage can of a human being must condemn him immediately.”

“You could convince me Hasan Piker is a GOP op. He’s an absolute soundbite machine for Republican ads!” wrote Alyssa Farah Griffin, a political strategist and co-host of ABC’s “The View.”

Piker responded to the clip of his remarks that was widely circulating on Thursday writing, “Oh this is why they were farming the interview.”

“I give a nuanced answer about acts of terror this admin has caused and they clickbait it,” he said. “He asked, i gave a nuanced answer. we’ve armed al qaeda since 9/11, we made its former commander the president of syria.”

“Our elites terrorize the entire world while ordinary Americans continue to foot the bill. we spent trillions ‘fighting’ the terror we created to provide cover for our oil barons stealing 3rd world resources,” Piker wrote in another post.

“It only amounted to more death overseas, more poverty at home. all while the MIC ballooned. no houses, no hospitals, no schools-just a growing crisis of homelessness, underemployment and diseases of despair in the wealthiest country on earth,” he wrote.

articles.title: Trump administration denies visas for Palestinian delegation to attend UN General Assembly for second year
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday denied visas to the Palestinian Liberation Organization (PLO) and the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in New York for the second time in more than a year. The State Department accused the PLO and the PA of failing their commitments as established in the PLO…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Wednesday denied visas to the Palestinian Liberation Organization (PLO) and the Palestinian Authority’s (PA) delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in New York for the second time in more than a year.

The State Department accused the PLO and the PA of failing their commitments as established in the PLO Commitments Compliance Act of 1989 and the Middle East Peace Commitments Act of 2002.

The alleged failures include “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ), seeking to bypass negotiations through seeking unilateral recognition, and continuing to pay stipends to terrorists and to glorify acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks,” State officials said in a statement .

The department said it will continue to provide waivers to the delegation, as part of the U.N. Headquarters Agreement. State officials concluded that denying the visas was “in our national interest to impose consequences and hold the PLO and PA accountable for glorifying terrorism

Officials with the PA’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates rejected the department’s claim that any recourse through the U.N., the ICC and the ICJ undermined peace efforts, rather that it was the PA’s legitimate right “and a peaceful, legal means to protect the Palestinian people and their rights,” according to a statement .

“The Ministry called upon the US administration to reconsider this decision, halt the policy of sanctions and restrictions, and engage in a direct, serious Palestinian-US dialogue to address any points of contention,” the statement reads. “It also urged the resumption of bilateral relations based on mutual respect and support for the implementation of the New York Declaration, relevant UN resolutions, and the peace plan—steps that would lead to ending the occupation and realizing an independent, sovereign State of Palestine with East Jerusalem as its capital.”

Visas were previously revoked in August 2025, when the State Department urged Palestinian leaders to condemn the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, which killed 1,200 Israelis and preceded the subsequent war carried out in the Gaza Strip. Israeli attacks killed more than 70,000 Palestinians and have destroyed much of Gaza’s infrastructure.

Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire agreement last October, but strikes deployed by the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) in Gaza as recently as Wednesday have displaced families while rescuers search for survivors in the rubble .

The department previously implored these groups to end attempts to have territories in the West Bank and Gaza Strip be recognized as a sovereign state.

President Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace has sought to have Israel withdraw from Gaza and Hamas hand over its weapons as part of a 15-point peace plan to eventually rehabilitate the territory. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the disarmament plan and objected to any establishment of a Palestinian state.

articles.title: Trump says he has a ‘big decision coming up’ on Iran
articles.summary: President Trump said on Thursday that he is facing a major looming decision in Iran as the U.S. war in the country shows no signs of subsiding. “I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything…
articles.body:
President Trump said on Thursday that he is facing a major looming decision in Iran as the U.S. war in the country shows no signs of subsiding.

“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios .

The comments come after reports surfaced that Trump is slated to meet with the leaders of six Gulf nations on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly next week.

Trump’s comments also come as energy prices spike in the U.S. as a result of the conflict.

The national average for gas prices jumped from $4.31 to $4.43 in the span of four days this week, according to AAA. Meanwhile the national average for diesel jumped 42 cents over the last week.

The issue is putting Republicans on the defensive in the upcoming midterm elections as Democrats hammer the Trump administration over affordability.

Trump told supporters on Wednesday in the North Carolina that higher gas prices are a “very inexpensive price to pay” for the war.

“Remember that. It’s a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more,” Trump said at a rally for GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley in Gastonia, N.C.

“But that’s going to come tumbling down,” he added, referring to gas prices. “That’s going to be like rocket ships in reverse.”
